title: The Fall of Sodom and the Rescue of Lot
summary: Two angels arrive in Sodom, and Lot takes them into his house. The men of the city surround the house and demand the guests, and the angels strike them blind and urge Lot's family to flee. The LORD rains sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah, Lot's wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt, and Lot escapes with his daughters, who later make him drunk and conceive the ancestors of Moab and Ammon.
story: Genesis 18 ended with Abraham pleading for Sodom down to ten righteous people. This chapter shows that there weren't ten. It also shows what became of Lot, who chose the well-watered plain near Sodom when he and Abraham separated (Genesis 13:10-13) and who now sits in the city's gate. The judgment falls, but God rescues Lot, not because Lot has earned it but because “He remembered Abraham” (verse 29). The chapter closes the Lot story and explains the origins of Moab and Ammon, two neighbors that Israel will deal with for centuries. Sodom itself becomes Scripture's standing example of sudden judgment.
historical:
Genesis places Sodom, Gomorrah, and Zoar in the plain of the Jordan near the Dead Sea (Genesis 13:10-12; 14:2-3), a region of salt, bitumen, and sulfur, where Genesis 14:10 mentions tar pits. Their exact sites are unknown. Some scholars have linked them with Early Bronze Age towns at the southeastern end of the Dead Sea, such as Bab edh-Dhra and Numeira; others have proposed Tall el-Hammam, northeast of the Dead Sea. Each identification has serious critics, and none is settled. Some have suggested natural mechanisms for the destruction, such as an earthquake igniting the region's bitumen and gases; the text presents it simply as the LORD's act. On Mount Sedom at the southwest of the Dead Sea, a salt pillar is popularly called Lot's wife, a later local name rather than evidence.

Moab and Ammon were real kingdoms east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea in the first millennium BC. The Mesha Stele, a Moabite inscription from about 840 BC, records a king of Moab's wars with Israel. The phrase “of today” in verses 37 and 38 shows the narrator writing when those peoples were well known.
cultural:
The city gate was where elders sat, trade happened, and legal disputes were settled, so Lot sitting there suggests he had gained some standing. The mob's taunt that he is “acting like a judge” (verse 9) shows how thin that standing was: he is still a foreigner. Lot takes the guests in, as custom required, and says they have come “under the protection of my roof” (verse 8), literally the shadow of his beam. His offer of his own daughters to the mob is appalling, and the narrator doesn't soften it; it shows how far the logic of a violent city has reached into the house of the man who is trying to resist it.

Scripture names Sodom's sin from several angles. Here it is the attempted gang rape of guests, the most extreme violation of hospitality. Ezekiel 16:49 says the city was “arrogant, overfed, and complacent; they did not help the poor and needy.” Jude 7 says Sodom and Gomorrah “indulged in sexual immorality and pursued strange flesh.” The outcry of Genesis 18:20 suggests victims. The biblical picture is of a city whose pride, excess, cruelty, and sexual violence had become its way of life.
literary: The chapter is written as a dark mirror of Genesis 18. Abraham received his guests at noon, ran, bowed, and served a feast; Lot receives them at evening, bows, and serves a meal, but the night ends in violence rather than promise. The story also echoes the flood: a righteous man and his family are rescued from a judgment that destroys everyone else, and afterward the father's drunkenness leads to shame involving his children (compare Genesis 9:20-27). Judges 19 later retells the pattern, in places nearly word for word, in the Israelite town of Gibeah, a sign that Israel itself could become Sodom. Within the chapter, the word overthrow gathers the judgment (verses 21, 25, 29), and the command not to look back sets up the fate of Lot's wife.

outline.t: Lot takes the two angels into his house
The men of Sodom surround the house
Warning, hesitation, and the flight to Zoar
Sodom and Gomorrah destroyed; Lot's wife looks back
Lot's daughters and the origins of Moab and Ammon

doctrines.note: God's judgment on Sodom is real, sudden, and total, and it comes after the outcry has been heard and investigated. Scripture uses the city again and again as a warning that God does not ignore cruelty forever.

Lot is rescued while he hesitates. The angels seize his hand and his family's and lead them out “because of the LORD's compassion for them” (verse 16). Rescue comes by mercy, not merit, and it is tied to God's faithfulness to Abraham.

Sin here is both social and personal. A whole city has normalized violence, and its influence reaches into Lot's household: his hesitation, his wife's backward look, and his daughters' scheme all show how deeply a place can shape the people who live in it.

words.note: Haphak, to turn, overturn, or overthrow. It is the key verb for the destruction of the cities (verses 21, 25, and 29), and a related noun, the “catastrophe” of verse 29, appears beside it. The prophets later speak of God overthrowing Sodom and Gomorrah as the standard picture of total judgment (Amos 4:11; Jeremiah 49:18).

Chemlah, compassion or pity, the feeling that moves someone to spare another. It is rare, and here it explains why a hesitating Lot is dragged out of the city at all. The rescue is an act of God's pity.

Zakar, to remember. In Scripture God's remembering is never a matter of recovering forgotten facts; it means acting on a commitment. God remembered Noah and the waters receded (Genesis 8:1); here he remembered Abraham and brought Lot out.

christ: Jesus uses this chapter to speak about his own coming. In Luke 17:28-32 he compares the days before the Son of Man is revealed to the days of Lot, when people ate, drank, bought, and built until fire fell, and he warns, “Remember Lot's wife!” The point is that attachment to the old life can keep a person from the rescue God provides. Jesus also said it would be more bearable for Sodom on the day of judgment than for towns that rejected him and his messengers (Matthew 10:15; 11:23-24), because they had seen more. The chapter's ending holds a quiet surprise: Moab, born here in shame, will produce Ruth, a Moabite woman who becomes the great-grandmother of David and is named in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). The line that seemed cut off from blessing is brought into the Messiah's own family.

hard.q: How can Scripture call Lot righteous when he offered his daughters to a mob?
hard.a:
Second Peter 2:7-8 calls Lot a righteous man distressed by the lawless conduct around him, and readers rightly ask how that fits this chapter. Lot offers his daughters to a violent crowd, hesitates when told to flee, bargains to go to a nearby town instead of the mountains, and ends his story drunk in a cave. Genesis reports all of this without praise.

Several things help. First, Genesis often records what people did without approving it; the reader is expected to see the horror of the offer, not to learn from it. Second, righteous in Scripture usually describes someone who stands in right relation to God and holds to him, not someone without sin. Lot resisted Sodom's demand, sheltered the guests, and believed the warning enough to leave; by the standard of the city, he was the one person who stood apart. Third, the chapter itself insists that he was saved by God's compassion and by God's remembrance of Abraham, not by his own merit. Lot is a picture of a believer badly compromised by the world he chose, and rescued anyway. The account of his daughters is best read as the tragic end of that compromise, not as a model.

questions: Lot chose Sodom because the land looked good (Genesis 13:10). What choices that seemed reasonable can slowly shape a person or a family in ways they didn't intend?
The angels had to take Lot by the hand because he hesitated. What makes it hard to leave something behind even when you know it is dangerous?
Moab begins in shame, yet Ruth the Moabite enters the family of Jesus. What does that say about the reach of God's grace?
